questions.question: An EOQ policy with constant demand rate $D$ repeats ordering cycles of length $t_0^*>0$, and each order arrives a fixed lead time $L\ge0$ after it is placed. With $n=\lfloor L/t_0^*\rfloor$, what does the effective lead time $L_e=L-nt_0^*$ measure?
options: The lead time $L$ minus exactly one cycle length $t_0^*$
The number of cycles that fit into the lead time $L$
The part of $L$ left after removing all complete cycles
The total length $nt_0^*$ of the complete cycles in $L$

questions.question: In a repeating EOQ policy, orders are spaced $t_0^*>0$ apart and each takes a fixed time $L\ge0$ to arrive. Which statement correctly describes the possible values of the effective lead time $L_e=L-\lfloor L/t_0^*\rfloor t_0^*$?
options: $0\le L_e<t_0^*$: every complete cycle that fits is removed, and no more.
$L_e$ can equal $t_0^*$ when $L$ is an exact multiple of the cycle.
$L_e$ can become negative when $L$ is just below a multiple of $t_0^*$.
$L_e$ can exceed $t_0^*$ when $L$ is much longer than one cycle.

questions.question: An EOQ policy with constant demand rate $D$ repeats ordering cycles of length $t_0^*>0$, and each order arrives a fixed lead time $L\ge0$ after it is placed. Suppose $L=20$ days, $t_0^*=7$ days and so the effective lead time is $L_e=6$ days. How long after it is placed does an order arrive?
For an EOQ policy whose delivery delay $L$ is shorter than its cycle length $t_0^*$, so that $0\le L<t_0^*$, what is the effective lead time $L_e=L-\lfloor L/t_0^*\rfloor t_0^*$?
options: $L_e=0$, as the order arrives within its cycle
$L_e=t_0^*-L$, the time left in the cycle
$L_e=L$, because no complete cycle fits into $L$

questions.question: An EOQ policy with constant demand rate $D$ repeats ordering cycles of length $t_0^*>0$, and each order arrives a fixed lead time $L\ge0$ after it is placed. Why may complete cycles be removed from $L$ when locating the ordering moment, so that only $L_e=L-\lfloor L/t_0^*\rfloor t_0^*$ matters?
options: Because the stock pattern repeats every $t_0^*$, so whole cycles change nothing.
Because the supplier ships faster when more than one cycle of demand is on order.
Because no demand occurs while orders from earlier cycles are still in transit.
Because holding cost is charged only during the last $L_e$ time units of the delay.

questions.question: An EOQ policy has an ordering cycle of $t_0^*=5$ days, and each order arrives $L=23$ days after it is placed. What is the effective lead time $L_e=L-\lfloor L/t_0^*\rfloor t_0^*$?
Orders under an EOQ policy are placed every 10 days and each one is delivered 4 days after it is placed. Compute the effective lead time $L_e$ of this policy.
An EOQ policy orders every 2 weeks, and the supplier delivers 30 days after each order. What is the effective lead time $L_e=L-\lfloor L/t_0^*\rfloor t_0^*$, in days?
An EOQ policy orders $y^*=300$ units each time, demand is $D=50$ units per week, and an order arrives $L=15$ weeks after it is placed. What is the effective lead time $L_e$?

Demand is $D=30$ units per day, each order of $y^*=120$ units starts a cycle of $t_0^*=4$ days, and the lead time is $L=10$ days. Stock falls linearly and each order is placed so that it arrives exactly when stock runs out. How many units are on hand when an order is placed?

An EOQ policy with constant demand rate $D$ repeats ordering cycles of length $t_0^*>0$, and each order arrives a fixed lead time $L\ge0$ after it is placed. Suppose $L=nt_0^*+L_e$ with $n=\lfloor L/t_0^*\rfloor\ge1$ and $0<L_e<t_0^*$. How many earlier orders are still in transit at the moment a new order is placed?

Under constant demand, an EOQ policy places orders every $t_0^*$ time units, and the supplier's delivery delay is exactly three cycles, $L=3t_0^*$. What are the effective lead time and the timing of each order?
options: $L_e=t_0^*$: each order is placed one full cycle before a stock-out.
$L_e=0$: each order is placed at a cycle boundary, when a batch arrives.
$L_e=0$: delivery becomes instantaneous, so no order is in transit.
$L_e$ is not defined, since $L/t_0^*$ has no fractional part.

questions.question: An EOQ policy with constant demand rate $D$ repeats ordering cycles of length $t_0^*>0$, and each order arrives a fixed lead time $L\ge0$ after it is placed. A student computes $n$ by rounding $L/t_0^*$ to the nearest whole number instead of using $n=\lfloor L/t_0^*\rfloor$. Why can this go wrong?
options: Rounding is the same as the floor, since $L/t_0^*$ is always a whole number.
If $L/t_0^*$ rounds up, $L-nt_0^*$ is negative and no ordering moment is located.
Rounding up is safer, since it orders earlier and so never causes shortages.
Rounding gives the same remainder, only shifted by a whole cycle.

questions.question: An EOQ policy has cycle length $t_0^*=7$ days. The supplier's lead time rises from $L=13$ to $L=15$ days. How does the effective lead time $L_e=L-\lfloor L/t_0^*\rfloor t_0^*$ change?
options: It falls from 6 days to 1 day
It rises from 6 days to 8 days
It rises from 13 days to 15 days

questions.question: An EOQ policy has setup cost $K=90$ per order, demand $D=20$ units per day and holding cost $h=1$ per unit per day, and each order arrives $L=10$ days after it is placed. What is the effective lead time $L_e$?

An EOQ policy has cycle length 7 weeks, with stock running out at weeks 7, 14, 21, 28 and so on, and each order arrives 20 weeks after it is placed, exactly at a stock-out. An order is placed at week 1. When does it arrive?
An EOQ policy orders $y^*=Dt_0^*$ units per cycle, stock falls linearly at rate $D$, and the lead time is $L>t_0^*$. Why can the order not be triggered when on-hand stock falls to $DL$ units?
options: On-hand stock never exceeds $y^*=Dt_0^*$, which is smaller than $DL$.
Stock $DL$ is reached, but ordering then gives too much stock on hand.
Triggering at $DL$ is valid, but raises holding cost above the EOQ level.
$DL$ is too low a trigger, so the order would arrive after a stock-out.

questions.question: An EOQ policy with constant demand rate $D$ repeats ordering cycles of length $t_0^*>0$, and each order arrives a fixed lead time $L\ge0$ after it is placed. Two possible lead times $L$ and $L'$ are compared for the same $t_0^*$. Which condition is necessary and sufficient for them to give the same effective lead time?
options: $L$ and $L'$ differ by less than one cycle $t_0^*$.
$L$ and $L'$ contain the same number $n$ of cycles.

questions.question: An EOQ policy has setup cost $K=50$, holding cost $h=1$ per unit per week and lead time $L=3.5$ weeks, and the EOQ $\sqrt{2KD/h}$ is used with cycle $t_0^*=\sqrt{2K/(Dh)}$. Demand rises from $D=25$ to $D=100$ units per week and the EOQ is recomputed. What is the new effective lead time?

Demand is $D=10$ units per week, each order of 70 units starts a 7-week cycle, and each order arrives $L=20$ weeks after it is placed, exactly when stock runs out. At the moment an order is placed, how many units are on hand plus already ordered but not yet received (not counting the new order)?
